claims.text: In LogRocket's measured benchmark, E2B took 717ms to create a sandbox and 662ms to resume from pause.
In LogRocket's measured benchmark, Daytona took 742ms to create a sandbox and 1254ms to resume, because its stop-then-start flow rebuilds more than a memory-preserving pause.
In LogRocket's measured benchmark, Modal took 2437ms to create a sandbox and 2347ms to boot from a snapshot; Modal has no in-place resume.
In LogRocket's measured benchmark, Vercel Sandbox took 1852ms to create and 3333ms to resume, the only platform where resume was slower than fresh create.
In LogRocket's measured benchmark, Blaxel took 2824ms to create a sandbox and 1924ms to resume from standby.
LogRocket's harness counted a sandbox as ready only when a command had actually executed inside it, not when the API acknowledged the request.

BeyondTrust research found AWS AgentCore's 'Sandbox' mode, which runs on Firecracker, still permitted outbound DNS A and AAAA queries; researchers built a DNS command-and-control channel and used an over-broad IAM role to read S3 buckets; AWS remediated DNS tunneling on April 15, 2026.

Cloudflare's Worker Loader runs code in a V8 isolate that starts in milliseconds but isolates only at the process level, while Cloudflare's container-based Sandbox SDK is a separate, stronger product.
Daytona runs Docker containers (shared host kernel) by default, with Kata or Sysbox available as opt-in stronger isolation.
Firecracker snapshot restore is cited at 5-30ms versus 125-200ms for a cold boot, with snapshots stored on local NVMe (target 2-5ms load time).

Spheron states gVisor's user-space kernel blocks direct PCIe GPU passthrough, whereas Firecracker supports VFIO passthrough to give a microVM near-native GPU access; Firecracker requires bare metal because nested virtualization adds 5-15ms per VM operation and blocks PCIe passthrough.
Spheron's Firecracker network setup gives each microVM a TAP device bridged on the host, with per-sandbox iptables FORWARD rules (physdev match) to drop all egress except allowlisted destinations.

Spheron lists Modal Sandboxes as gVisor (runsc) with 100-300ms cold start and T4/A10G GPU support, and Daytona as Docker + gVisor with 200-500ms cold start (this conflicts with other sources describing Daytona as container-by-default).
E2B's docs cite about 150 ms startup from a snapshot or custom template and about 1 second to resume a paused sandbox; pausing saves filesystem and memory.

E2B pricing is $0.000014 per vCPU-second and $0.0000045 per GiB-second (default 2 vCPU/4 GiB), Pro is $150/month with 24-hour sessions and 100 concurrent sandboxes, Hobby is limited to 1-hour sessions and 20 concurrent sandboxes.
E2B egress can be controlled by CIDR or hostname, and a secrets vault injects credentials at the egress proxy.

Modal Sandboxes run on gVisor or a VM runtime, default to a 5-minute lifetime adjustable to 24 hours, and are billed at CPU $0.00003942/core-second and memory $0.00000667/GiB-second at non-preemptible rates (3x list).

Daytona states sandboxes spin up in under 90 ms; it bills $0.0504/vCPU-hour and $0.0162/GiB-hour memory, offers network controls (block all or allow CIDRs/domains), and auto-stops after 15 minutes idle by default.

Cloudflare states each Sandbox SDK container instance is a microVM with its own kernel and network, and Dynamic Workers can block outbound requests with globalOutbound: null; Cloudflare recommends keeping credentials in the Worker so they are added to outbound requests after leaving the sandbox.
Fly.io Sprites pause after about 30 seconds idle, with a warm wake of 100 to 500 ms and a cold wake of 1 to 2 seconds.
Vercel Sandbox bills $0.128 per Active CPU hour and $0.0212 per GB-hour of memory, and its firewall supports deny-all or domain/CIDR allowlists with credentials brokering.
Upstash lists Cloudflare Sandbox cold start at 1-3s, with the container in its own VM, sleeping after 10 minutes idle and retaining nothing by default except directory backups to R2.
AWS Lambda MicroVMs use Firecracker, preserve memory and disk across suspend for up to 8 hours, and independent testing clocked roughly 2 seconds to RUNNING; AWS publishes no latency figures.

A 1 vCPU/2 GB sandbox costs $0.126/hour on AWS MicroVMs versus $0.083/hour on Daytona and E2B (E2B adds a $150/month base fee); AWS also charges $0.08/GB-month snapshot storage, about $962/month for a 1,000-VM hibernating fleet.
Firecracker boots in ~125ms with under 5 MiB memory overhead per VM and up to 150 VMs per second per host; gVisor adds 10-30% overhead on I/O-heavy workloads; Kata Containers boot in ~200ms.
